This concept, garnering significant CGI praise, is unprecedented for a major automobile company to offer such a system—and it cleverly distinguishes the Yeti from its rivals.
Another area where the Yeti takes a different approach is in cabin materials.
Created collaboratively by Skoda’s design team and Volkswagen’s RCD division in Czech, its soft-touch interior mirrors the design of sister Audi models, including the A1, A4, and A6.
The canvas-textured materials look and feel like natural surroundings, differing only subtly from the version used in the base models.
On a chilly and gloomy November afternoon, it is evident that the Yeti belongs to the same lineage as other Volkswagen Group models, and finding its cabin fitting into the range comes as no surprise.
The proper arrangement of three rows of buttons for the gearbox, lights, hazards, and wipers – instead found deep in the centre console – implies that the driver might be eager to test the Yeti's capabilities.
Out on the road the Yeti displays all the traits one expects of the Volkswagen Group.
The gearbox is skillfully designed with a throw of a tastefully positioned lever that feels exceptionally lightweight, making it clear why this system was successful in the Audi A4.
While power sent to the front wheels isn't inexpensive given the engine's displacement of merely 2.0 liters, it wouldn't be accurate to suggest the Yeti lacks power since it possesses substantial torque reserves.
Both the smart-idle stop-start system, which disables the engine during idling and reactivates it when the throttle is opened, and a six-speed gearbox featuring Tiptronic, contribute to the Yeti’s notable fuel efficiency, achieving gains of 5.6 mpg.
